notes.definition: Water and nitrogen balance means keeping the water and ion content of the body within safe limits and removing nitrogen waste. The kidneys do this by filtering the blood and selectively reabsorbing useful substances, producing urine that contains urea, excess water and excess ions.
explanation: Water leaves the body in three main ways. Water is lost from the lungs during exhalation, and water, ions and urea are lost from the skin in sweat. There is no control over how much water, ions or urea are lost through the lungs and skin. Excess water, ions and urea are removed by the kidneys in the urine, and this is the route the body can control.

Keeping body fluids at the right concentration matters because cells are surrounded by tissue fluid. If body fluids become too dilute, water moves into cells by osmosis and the cells may swell and burst. If body fluids become too concentrated, water moves out of cells by osmosis and they shrink. In both cases cells do not function efficiently.

Nitrogen waste comes from protein. Proteins in food are digested into amino acids. The body cannot store excess amino acids, so in the liver they are deaminated: the amino (nitrogen-containing) part is removed and forms ammonia. Ammonia is toxic, so the liver immediately converts it into urea, which is much less toxic. Urea travels in the blood plasma to the kidneys for excretion.

The kidneys produce urine in two stages. First, blood is filtered under pressure, so small molecules such as water, glucose, ions and urea pass out of the blood into the kidney tubule. Large molecules such as proteins and cells stay in the blood. Second, useful substances are selectively reabsorbed back into the blood: all of the glucose, some of the ions and as much water as the body needs. Urea, excess ions and excess water form urine, which is stored in the bladder.

Kidney failure means the kidneys cannot remove urea and excess water and ions, so they build up in the blood. It can be treated by kidney dialysis or a kidney transplant. In dialysis, the patient's blood flows past dialysis fluid separated by a partially permeable membrane. The fluid contains the same concentration of glucose and useful ions as normal blood plasma but no urea, so urea, excess ions and excess water diffuse out of the blood while glucose is not lost.

A kidney transplant gives a permanent, working kidney from a donor. The donor tissue type must closely match the patient's, and the patient must take immunosuppressant drugs for life to stop the immune system rejecting the new kidney. These drugs increase the risk of infections. There are not enough donor kidneys, so many patients stay on dialysis, which needs several long sessions every week and a controlled diet.

Higher tier: the water level of the blood is controlled by the hormone ADH (antidiuretic hormone). When the blood is too concentrated, the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood. ADH acts on the kidney tubules, making them more permeable, so more water is reabsorbed back into the blood. A small volume of concentrated urine is produced. When the blood is too dilute, less ADH is released. This is controlled by negative feedback.
keyFacts: Water is lost from the lungs (exhaled air), the skin (sweat) and the kidneys (urine).
There is no control over water, ion or urea loss from the lungs and skin; the kidneys provide the control.
Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver to form ammonia.
Ammonia is toxic, so the liver converts it to urea for safe excretion.
Kidneys filter the blood, then selectively reabsorb all glucose, some ions and some water.
Urine contains urea, excess water and excess ions, and normally no glucose or protein.
If body fluids are too dilute, cells gain water by osmosis and may burst; too concentrated and they lose water and shrink.
Dialysis fluid has the same glucose and useful ion concentrations as normal plasma but no urea.
Kidney transplant patients take immunosuppressant drugs to prevent rejection.
Higher: ADH from the pituitary gland makes kidney tubules reabsorb more water.

keyTerms.definition: The removal of the amino group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia.
The less toxic nitrogen waste made in the liver from ammonia and excreted by the kidneys in urine.
The first stage of urine production: small molecules (water, glucose, ions, urea) are forced out of the blood into the kidney tubule.
Taking back useful substances (all glucose, some ions, the water the body needs) from the kidney tubule into the blood.
Treatment for kidney failure in which blood passes alongside dialysis fluid across a partially permeable membrane so that urea and excess ions and water diffuse out.
A drug that reduces the activity of the immune system, used to stop a transplanted organ being rejected.
Higher tier: a hormone released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated; it increases water reabsorption in the kidney tubules.
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of filtered water reabsorbed
workedExamples.question: The kidneys filter 180 dm³ of fluid a day. A person produces 1.5 dm³ of urine a day. Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed. Assume urine is all water.
workedExamples.answer: 99.2 % of the filtered water is reabsorbed.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting filtrate and urine data
workedExamples.question: Concentrations in g per 100 cm³: blood plasma glucose 0.10, urea 0.03, protein 8.0. Filtrate glucose 0.10, urea 0.03, protein 0. Urine glucose 0, urea 2.0, protein 0. Explain the protein and glucose values, and calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in urine than in plasma.
steps: Protein is 0 in the filtrate: protein molecules are too large to be filtered out of the blood.
Glucose is in the filtrate (it is small enough to be filtered) but is 0 in the urine: all of it is reabsorbed into the blood.
Urea becomes concentrated because most of the water is reabsorbed but urea is not.
workedExamples.answer: Urea is about 67 times more concentrated in urine than in plasma.

workedExamples.title: Unit conversion: mass of glucose filtered
workedExamples.question: Filtrate contains 0.1 g of glucose per 100 cm³. 180 dm³ of filtrate is produced each day. Calculate the mass of glucose filtered per day.
steps: Convert dm³ to cm³: 180 dm³ × 1000 = 180 000 cm³
workedExamples.answer: 180 g of glucose is filtered each day, and in a healthy person all of it is reabsorbed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think urea is made in the kidneys.
misconceptions.right: In fact urea is made in the liver from ammonia. The kidneys only remove urea from the blood.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the kidneys only filter out waste.
misconceptions.right: In fact filtration removes useful substances too (glucose, ions, water). Selective reabsorption then takes the useful ones back into the blood.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think dialysis fluid is pure water.
misconceptions.right: In fact dialysis fluid contains glucose and ions at normal plasma concentrations, so glucose and useful ions do not diffuse out of the blood. It contains no urea, so urea does diffuse out.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think ADH makes you produce more urine.
misconceptions.right: In fact ADH makes the tubules reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is made. Anti-diuretic means 'against urine production'.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think sweating and breathing out are the main ways the body controls its water level.
misconceptions.right: In fact there is no control over water loss from the lungs and skin; the kidneys adjust the urine to balance water.

realWorld: People with kidney failure often have haemodialysis at a hospital three times a week for about four hours each time, and must limit salt, potassium and fluid in their diet.
The UK uses an opt-out organ donation system, partly to increase the number of donor kidneys and reduce waiting times for transplants.
Athletes who sweat heavily can lose a lot of ions, so sports drinks replace both water and ions.
Urine colour is a quick, rough indicator of hydration: pale urine suggests plenty of water, dark urine suggests the body is conserving water.
higherTier: The water level in the body is controlled by the hormone ADH, which acts on the kidney tubules.
ADH is released by the pituitary gland when the blood is too concentrated and causes more water to be reabsorbed back into the blood from the kidney tubules.
When the blood is too dilute, less ADH is released, so less water is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced.
This is controlled by negative feedback.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is assessed only in separate Biology (8461), not in Combined Science Trilogy: water loss routes, osmotic effects on cells, deamination and urea, kidney filtration and selective reabsorption, ADH (Higher), dialysis and kidney transplants.
examTips: Always say ALL glucose is reabsorbed but only SOME ions and SOME water. Examiners reward that precision.
When explaining dialysis, link each substance to its concentration gradient: no urea in the fluid so urea diffuses out; equal glucose concentration so there is no net movement of glucose.
For ADH questions, follow the chain: blood too concentrated, more ADH from the pituitary, tubules reabsorb more water, small volume of concentrated urine, blood concentration returns to normal.
Do not write that the kidneys 'make' urea. Write that the liver makes urea and the kidneys excrete it.
In 'evaluate' questions on dialysis versus transplant, give advantages and disadvantages of both and finish with a justified conclusion.
summary: Water leaves via lungs, skin and kidneys; only the kidneys give control.
Osmotic changes in body fluids can make cells swell and burst or shrink.
Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver; ammonia is converted to urea.
Kidneys filter blood and selectively reabsorb glucose, some ions and water.
Urine contains urea, excess water and excess ions.
Kidney failure is treated by dialysis or a transplant, each with drawbacks.
Higher: ADH from the pituitary increases water reabsorption, by negative feedback.

flashcards.front: Name three ways water leaves the body.
flashcards.back: Exhaled from the lungs, sweat from the skin, urine from the kidneys.

flashcards.front: Which water loss route can the body control?
flashcards.back: The kidneys (urine). There is no control over loss from the lungs and skin.

flashcards.front: What is deamination and where does it happen?
flashcards.back: Removal of the amino group from excess amino acids to form ammonia, in the liver.

flashcards.front: Why is ammonia converted to urea?
flashcards.back: Ammonia is toxic; urea is much less toxic and can be safely carried in the blood to the kidneys.

flashcards.front: What are the two stages of urine production?
flashcards.back: Filtration of the blood, then selective reabsorption of useful substances.

flashcards.front: What is selectively reabsorbed in the kidney?
flashcards.back: All of the glucose, some ions and as much water as the body needs.
Urea, excess water and excess ions.

flashcards.front: What happens to cells if body fluids are too dilute?
flashcards.back: Water enters them by osmosis; they swell and may burst.

flashcards.front: What happens to cells if body fluids are too concentrated?
flashcards.back: Water leaves them by osmosis; they shrink and do not work properly.
Glucose and useful ions at the same concentration as normal plasma, and no urea.

flashcards.front: Why does urea leave the blood in dialysis?
flashcards.back: It diffuses down its concentration gradient across the partially permeable membrane into fluid that has no urea.

flashcards.front: Two disadvantages of a kidney transplant?
flashcards.back: Risk of rejection, lifelong immunosuppressants increase infection risk, shortage of donors, surgical risks.

flashcards.front: Higher: Which gland releases ADH and when?
flashcards.back: The pituitary gland, when the blood is too concentrated.
Makes the kidney tubules reabsorb more water into the blood, giving a small volume of concentrated urine.

questions.question: Which organ removes excess water, ions and urea from the blood?
markScheme: 1 mark: Kidneys
questions.explanation: The kidneys filter the blood and adjust urine. The lungs and skin also lose water but there is no control over these losses. The liver makes urea but does not remove it from the body.

questions.question: In which organ is urea made?
markScheme: 1 mark: Liver
questions.explanation: Excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver and the ammonia formed is converted to urea there. The kidneys only excrete urea; the bladder only stores urine.

questions.question:
Some useful substances are taken back into the blood from the kidney tubules.
What is this process called?
markScheme: 1 mark: Selective reabsorption
questions.explanation: Filtration is the first stage, when small molecules leave the blood. Selective reabsorption returns the useful ones. Deamination happens in the liver. Excretion is removal of waste from the body.

questions.question:
Water leaves the body in several ways.
Which way of losing water can the body control?
options: Water lost in sweat for cooling as well as balance
Water lost from the lungs during exercise
markScheme: 1 mark: Water in urine
questions.explanation: The AQA specification states there is no control over water, ion or urea loss by the lungs and skin. The kidneys adjust the volume and concentration of urine to keep water balance.

questions.question: What is meant by deamination?
options: Joining amino acids together to make proteins
Filtering amino acids out of the blood in the kidney
Removing the amino group from excess amino acids to form ammonia
markScheme: 1 mark: Removing the amino group from excess amino acids to form ammonia
questions.explanation: Deamination happens in the liver because excess amino acids cannot be stored. The nitrogen-containing part becomes ammonia, which is then converted to urea. The reverse (urea to ammonia) does not happen in the body.

questions.question: Which substance is filtered out of the blood in the kidney and is normally all reabsorbed?
markScheme: 1 mark: Glucose
questions.explanation: All glucose is reabsorbed in a healthy person, so urine contains no glucose. Only some water and some ions are reabsorbed, depending on the body's needs. Urea is mostly left in the tubule to be excreted.

questions.question:
A person's blood plasma becomes much too concentrated.
What happens to the person's body cells?
options: Water moves out of the cells by osmosis and the cells shrink
Water moves into the cells by osmosis and the cells burst
Glucose moves out of the cells by osmosis
The cells are not affected because they have cell walls
markScheme: 1 mark: Water moves out of the cells by osmosis and the cells shrink
questions.explanation: Water moves from the more dilute solution (inside the cell) to the more concentrated solution (outside). Animal cells have no cell wall. Osmosis is the movement of water, not glucose.

questions.question: Which statement describes the effect of ADH?
options: It decreases the permeability of the kidney tubules so more water is lost in urine
It increases the rate of filtration in the kidney
It increases the permeability of the kidney tubules so more water is reabsorbed into the blood
It makes the liver convert more ammonia into urea
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases the permeability of the kidney tubules so more water is reabsorbed into the blood
questions.explanation: ADH acts on the kidney tubules. More ADH means more water is reabsorbed, so urine is concentrated and small in volume. It does not affect filtration or the liver.

questions.question: Which gland releases ADH?
markScheme: 1 mark: Pituitary gland
questions.explanation: ADH is released by the pituitary gland in the brain when the blood is too concentrated. The thyroid releases thyroxine, the adrenal glands release adrenaline and the pancreas releases insulin and glucagon.

questions.question: What does the dialysis fluid used in kidney dialysis contain?
options: No glucose and no ions, so they are removed from the blood
The same concentration of glucose and useful ions as normal blood plasma, and no urea
markScheme: 1 mark: The same concentration of glucose and useful ions as normal blood plasma, and no urea
questions.explanation: Matching the glucose and useful ion concentrations means there is no net loss of them from the blood. Having no urea creates a concentration gradient so urea diffuses out of the blood. Pure water would draw glucose and ions out of the blood.

questions.question:
Before a kidney transplant, doctors check that the donor's tissue type closely matches the patient's tissue type.
Why?
options: To reduce the risk of the patient's immune system rejecting the kidney
To make sure the kidney is the right size
So the patient does not need any further treatment
To stop the kidney producing urea
markScheme: 1 mark: To reduce the risk of the patient's immune system rejecting the kidney
questions.explanation: Antigens on donor cells that differ from the patient's are recognised as foreign. A close match reduces this, but patients still need immunosuppressant drugs. Kidneys do not produce urea.

questions.question:
On a hot day a student exercises and drinks very little.
How will the student's urine be different from their urine on a cool day?
options: larger in volume and more dilute
larger in volume and more concentrated
smaller in volume and more concentrated
smaller in volume and more dilute
markScheme: 1 mark: smaller in volume and more concentrated
questions.explanation: More water is lost in sweat, so the kidneys reabsorb more water. Less water is left in the tubule, so less urine is made and the urea in it is more concentrated.

questions.question:
Water leaves the body in urine.
Name two other ways that water leaves the body.
markScheme: 1 mark: from the lungs in exhaled air / breathing out
1 mark: from the skin in sweat
questions.explanation: Water evaporates into the air in the lungs and is breathed out, and sweat glands release sweat containing water, ions and urea. Neither route is controlled for water balance.

questions.question:
Ammonia made in the liver is converted into urea.
Give the reason why.
markScheme: 1 mark: ammonia is toxic (urea is less toxic)
questions.explanation: Ammonia is toxic even at low concentrations, so it is converted straight away to urea, which is much less toxic and can be carried safely in the blood to the kidneys.

questions.question: Describe how urea is produced in the body from protein in the diet.
markScheme: 1 mark: protein is digested into amino acids
1 mark: excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, forming ammonia
1 mark: ammonia is converted into urea (in the liver)
questions.explanation: The body cannot store excess amino acids. Deamination in the liver removes the amino group as ammonia, which is converted to urea for excretion by the kidneys.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the concentrations of three substances in the blood plasma, in the filtrate in the kidney tubule and in the urine of a healthy person.
Glucose is filtered out of the blood in the kidney, but the urine contains no glucose.
Explain why.

headers: Concentration in blood plasma in g per 100 cm³
Concentration in filtrate in g per 100 cm³
Concentration in urine in g per 100 cm³

markScheme: 1 mark: glucose is small enough to be filtered out
1 mark: all of the glucose is (selectively) reabsorbed back into the blood
questions.explanation: Table 1 shows glucose at the same concentration in the filtrate as in the plasma, so it is filtered out (it is a small molecule). Filtration is not selective by usefulness, only by size. Selective reabsorption then returns all of the glucose to the blood, so its concentration in urine is 0. Protein is too large to be filtered at all.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows how a dialysis machine works.
Explain why the dialysis fluid contains no urea.

markScheme: 1 mark: creates a concentration gradient (higher urea in blood than fluid)
1 mark: so urea diffuses out of the blood into the dialysis fluid (across the membrane)
questions.explanation: Diffusion needs a concentration gradient. With no urea in the fluid, urea always moves from the blood (high concentration) into the fluid (low concentration).

questions.question: Give two disadvantages of treating kidney failure with a kidney transplant.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any two: risk of rejection; must take immunosuppressant drugs for life; immunosuppressants increase risk of infection; shortage of donor kidneys / long wait; risks of major surgery
questions.explanation: A transplant can restore normal kidney function, but the immune system may attack the donor organ, the drugs that prevent this weaken defence against pathogens, and few kidneys are available.

markScheme: 1 mark: blood becomes too dilute (water level too high), so the pituitary releases less ADH
1 mark: kidney tubules become less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed into the blood
1 mark: so a large volume of dilute urine is produced
questions.explanation: Figure 1 shows the volume of urine rising to a peak at about 60 minutes after drinking. The extra water makes the blood too dilute, so the pituitary gland releases less ADH. The kidney tubules become less permeable, so less water is reabsorbed and a large volume of dilute urine is produced. This is negative feedback: the rise in blood water level causes a response that lowers it again. Saying 'no ADH' is not quite right; secretion falls.

markScheme: 1 mark: a concentration gradient (of urea) is maintained along the whole length of the membrane
1 mark: so more urea (and excess ions) diffuses out of the blood
questions.explanation: As blood loses urea it meets fresher fluid with even less urea, so diffusion continues all the way along. If both flowed the same way, the concentrations could become equal and diffusion would stop.

questions.question:
A patient's blood plasma becomes too dilute.
Explain the effect on the patient's body cells.
markScheme: 1 mark: the cytoplasm is more concentrated than the plasma / tissue fluid
1 mark: so water moves into the cells by osmosis
1 mark: cells swell and may burst / do not function efficiently
questions.explanation: Osmosis moves water from the dilute solution to the more concentrated one through the partially permeable cell membrane. Animal cells have no cell wall to resist swelling.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the volume of fluid filtered by the kidneys of an adult each day and the volume of urine produced each day.
Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: volume reabsorbed = 180 − 1.5 = 178.5 dm³
questions.explanation: 178.5 ÷ 180 = 0.99167, × 100 = 99.17 %, which is 99.2 % to 3 significant figures. A common error is to calculate 1.5 ÷ 180 × 100 = 0.83 %, which is the percentage lost as urine.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the volume of water a person lost in one day.
Calculate the percentage of the total water loss that was lost in urine.

headers: Volume of water lost in cm³

questions.explanation: Add all the losses first to get the total, then divide the urine volume by the total. 1500 ÷ 2500 = 0.6, which is 60 %.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the concentration of urea in blood plasma and in urine.
Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the blood plasma.
Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

headers: Concentration of urea in g per 100 cm³

questions.explanation: 2.0 ÷ 0.03 = 66.67, which rounds to 67. Urea becomes concentrated because most water is reabsorbed from the tubule but most urea is not.

questions.question:
A patient has dialysis 3 times a week.
Each session lasts 4 hours.
Calculate the total time the patient spends on dialysis in one year.
There are 52 weeks in one year.
markScheme: 1 mark: 3 × 4 = 12 hours per week
1 mark: 12 × 52 = 624 hours
questions.explanation: 12 hours a week for 52 weeks is 624 hours. This large time commitment is one disadvantage of dialysis compared with a transplant.

questions.question:
Kidney filtrate contains 0.1 g of glucose per 100 cm³.
The kidneys produce 180 dm³ of filtrate per day.
Calculate the mass of glucose filtered per day.
markScheme: 1 mark: 180 dm³ = 180 000 cm³
questions.explanation: Convert to cm³ first (× 1000). 180 000 ÷ 100 = 1800 portions of 100 cm³, each with 0.1 g, giving 180 g. Forgetting the conversion gives 0.18 g.

questions.question: Describe how the kidneys produce urine from blood.
markScheme: Indicative content: blood is filtered in the kidney; small molecules (water, glucose, ions, urea) pass into the tubule; large molecules such as proteins and blood cells stay in the blood; all glucose is selectively reabsorbed; some ions are reabsorbed; water is reabsorbed according to the body's needs; urea is not reabsorbed (most stays in the tubule); urine contains urea, excess water and excess ions; urine is stored in the bladder.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear, sequenced description of both filtration and selective reabsorption, naming what is filtered and what is reabsorbed.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. kidneys filter blood or urine contains urea, without a clear sequence.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Top answers name both stages and are precise about 'all' glucose versus 'some' ions and water, and explain why protein is absent.

questions.question:
Kidney failure can be treated by dialysis or by a kidney transplant.
Evaluate these two treatments.
markScheme: Indicative content, dialysis: available without waiting for a donor; no risk of rejection; no immunosuppressant drugs; removes urea, excess ions and excess water by diffusion; but several sessions a week of several hours each; strict diet and fluid limits; risk of infection or blood clots at access site; expensive over many years; does not cure the problem.

Transplant: permanent working kidney; freedom from dialysis sessions and diet restrictions; cheaper in the long term; but shortage of donors and long waiting lists; tissue type must match; risk of rejection; lifelong immunosuppressants increase infection risk; risks of major surgery; donor kidney may fail eventually.
Conclusion: a justified judgement, e.g. a transplant is better for quality of life if a matched kidney is available, while dialysis keeps patients alive while waiting.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed advantages and disadvantages of both treatments and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some advantages and disadvantages of both, or detailed for one; conclusion may be missing or unsupported.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple points about one or both treatments.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: 'Evaluate' needs both sides and a conclusion. Linking points to the patient (time, diet, infection risk) scores higher than lists.

questions.question:
On a hot day a runner sweats a lot and drinks very little.
Explain how the body keeps the water content of the blood within normal limits.
Refer to ADH in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: water is lost in sweat (and from lungs) with no control; blood becomes too concentrated; this is detected by receptors in the brain; the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood; ADH travels in the blood to the kidneys; ADH acts on the kidney tubules making them more permeable to water; more water is reabsorbed back into the blood; a small volume of concentrated urine is produced; blood water concentration returns towards normal; when it is normal, ADH release falls; this is negative feedback; cells are protected from shrinking by osmosis.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): full, logically linked sequence from stimulus to response including the pituitary, ADH, tubules, reabsorption, urine and negative feedback.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most steps present, some links missing or negative feedback not explained.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): isolated points, e.g. more ADH or less urine.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good answer reads like a chain of cause and effect. Many students lose marks by saying ADH 'makes less urine' without explaining increased water reabsorption by the tubules.
